title: De altitudine columnarum sub proprio pondere corruentium

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E510 treats a vertical elastic column of height h (the transcription of the previous page writes b where it means the height) loaded by its own weight. It is held so that its axis passes through the base A (x = 0) and through the top (x = h), with y = 0 at both ends. An auxiliary horizontal force C is applied, and g is the horizontal offset (the interval GO) that enters the moment balance.

The previous page reduced the equilibrium condition to the integro-differential equation
(C/2bb + g) x − C x²/(2b³) + ∫₀ˣ x dy + e b² y'' = 0.
Here e·b⁴ = E k² is the bending stiffness; differentiating once gives a third-order linear ODE of Airy type.

Rules for building the power-series solution: ∫x dy vanishes at x = 0; y(0) = 0; and y ≈ αx near A. On this page Euler stresses that the free slope α 'exhibits the whole effect' of the horizontal force C. The series y(x; α, g, C) is therefore linear in the three parameters α, g, C.

§23: Imposing y(h) = 0 gives one linear relation among α, g, C and the material and geometric constants. It cannot yet fix α, because g is unknown.

The second relation comes from the definition g = (1/h)∫₀ʰ y dx. In §24 this is evaluated from the series, giving g·h = (linear form in α, g, C). Eliminating g between the two relations gives α as a function of C, of the form α = K(h, e, b)·C.

§25 (next page): there are special cases where α ≠ 0 even though C = 0. These are the critical heights at which the column begins to bend under its own weight. In modern terms, the determinant of the homogeneous linear system vanishes: an eigenvalue condition, equivalently the lateral compliance becoming unbounded.

The next page notes the threefold structure of the series coefficients: powers 3n+2 vanish, powers 3n+1 are proportional to α, and powers 3n are proportional to g. This is the hallmark of Airy-type equations, later solved by Greenhill (1881) with Bessel functions of order ±1/3.
errors: No mathematical error on this page; it is a procedural description of a linear eigenvalue (shooting-type) problem.

Calling α 'the angle itself, as it is to be regarded as infinitely small' is the standard linearization; it is correct only for infinitesimal deflection, which is all that is needed for the onset of buckling.

Whether Euler's later evaluation of the critical height in E510 is numerically and physically correct (boundary conditions, the meaning of g) is not decided on this page. I am unsure of the detailed later judgement (e.g. by Truesdell) on E510's final result.

ideas.what: Determining the critical height as the case where the linear relation between the lateral force C and the end slope α admits α ≠ 0 at C = 0: a vanishing determinant of a homogeneous linear boundary-value system.
ideas.modern_name: Eigenvalue / bifurcation (adjacent-equilibrium) criterion for buckling; equivalently divergence of lateral compliance
ideas.where_published: E65 (Methodus inveniendi, Additamentum I), E238, E508/E509/E510 (Acta Acad. Petrop. 1778)

ideas.what: Handling the nonlocal unknown g by expressing it through the mean deflection (1/h)∫y dx, i.e. adding an integral side condition and eliminating the extra parameter.
ideas.modern_name: Integral (nonlocal) constraint in a boundary-value problem; shooting with parameter elimination
ideas.where_published: E510 itself and related column papers

ideas.what: Power-series solution with free initial slope α as the shooting parameter.

deep.surprise_reason: The page only sets out the solution procedure: the boundary condition y(h) = 0, elimination of g through ∫y dx, and α as a function of C. That buckling arises when α survives at C = 0 is Euler's well-known eigenvalue criterion, and the heavy-column problem in E510 is well documented in the history of elastic stability (Truesdell; Greenhill 1881).
transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image essentially; the height symbol appears as h on this page ('x = h'), whereas the previous page's transcription uses b in places (amplitude bb, M = bbb). This is a notational inconsistency to check against the original, not an error on this page.
'ſcilicet integrale ∫y dx a termino x = 0 vſque ad terminum x = h fuerit extenſum' is correctly read.
